room_start.narration: The morning light barely reaches your desk through the dusty window. Your schoolbooks are open — mathematics, your favorite. Outside, voices rise and fall like the tide. Your mother calls someone's name. Not yours. Not yet.

choices.label: Ask to go to school tomorrow

room_study.narration: You lower your head and trace the numbers with your finger. Each equation is a small door to somewhere else. For a moment, the voices outside fade. You solve one problem, then another. The pencil feels steady in your hand. This is yours. This moment, at least, is yours.
room_study.emotionalResponse: A quiet defiance settles in your chest.

room_help.narration: You close the book carefully, marking your page with a folded corner. The kitchen needs water. The floor needs sweeping. Your hands know this work — they have done it every day since you were small enough to hold a broom. Your mother nods but does not smile. This is expected, not praised.
room_help.emotionalResponse: You are useful. That is something.

room_school.narration: "Can I go to school tomorrow?" The words leave your mouth like birds released from a cage. Your mother pauses. She looks at you the way she looks at the rain — something natural that cannot be helped. "We'll see," she says. In your family, 'we'll see' has never once meant yes.
room_school.emotionalResponse: Hope is a muscle you keep exercising, even when it aches.

pressure_intro.narration: Days blur together. Then one evening, the house fills with people you recognize but rarely see. Aunts. Uncles. A woman you don't know, watching you from the corner with measuring eyes. Tea is served in the good cups — the ones usually locked in the cabinet. No one has told you why they are here. No one needs to.

choices.label: Speak up and ask what's happening
Find your mother and ask for help

pressure_speak.narration: "What is everyone talking about?" The room does not go silent — that would give you too much power. Instead, the conversation shifts around you like water around a stone. Your uncle smiles. "Children's questions," he says, and the adults laugh. But the woman in the corner is not laughing. She is still watching you, and now she is nodding.
pressure_speak.emotionalResponse: Your courage hits a wall you cannot see.

pressure_quiet.narration: You sit in the doorway where shadows meet light. Words drift toward you in fragments: "good family," "old enough," "better than waiting." Your aunt says something about a "generous offer." Your mother's silence is the loudest sound in the room. You press your back against the wall and make yourself small. Small enough, maybe, to disappear.
pressure_quiet.emotionalResponse: Silence does not protect you. It only makes you invisible.

pressure_mother.narration: You find her in the kitchen, her hands busy with nothing. "Mama, what's happening?" She pulls you close — too close, too tight, the way you hold something you're about to let go of. "It will be fine," she says into your hair. "Everything will be fine." Her voice shakes on the word 'fine' like a bridge under too much weight.
pressure_mother.emotionalResponse: She loves you. That was never the question. The question is whether love is enough.

escape_intro.narration: A week passes. The visitors leave, but their words stay behind like smoke in curtains. You hear the date mentioned once, then quickly silenced when someone sees you listening. You know what is coming. Your body knows it the way animals know a storm. You have a window. It is closing.

choices.label: Talk to your teacher at school
Hide your school papers as proof you're a student
Promise to work harder to prove your worth at home

escape_teacher.narration: Your teacher listens. She truly listens — leaning forward, her brow folding with something that might be pain. "I understand," she says. And you believe her. She writes a note. She says she will talk to someone. She touches your shoulder. When you come back the next day, there is a different teacher at the desk. No one explains why. The note is gone. The shoulder that held you is gone.
escape_teacher.emotionalResponse: The system has many hands, and they do not all reach toward you.

escape_hide.narration: You gather your papers — every test, every marked assignment, every star your teacher drew in red ink. You hide them under your mattress like treasure. Like proof. If they can see how good you are, how much you've learned, surely that changes something? But when the day comes, no one asks to see your papers. No one asks what you know. What you know was never the currency that mattered.
escape_hide.emotionalResponse: Merit is meaningless in a market that trades in daughters.

escape_work.narration: You wake before dawn. You carry water until your arms burn. You cook, you clean, you make yourself indispensable. If they need you here, they cannot send you there. That is the logic. It is a child's logic, and it breaks the way children's things break — completely, and without anyone noticing. "She'll make a good wife," your aunt says, watching you work. "See how capable she is." Your labor becomes the advertisement for your own removal.
escape_work.emotionalResponse: Even your resistance becomes evidence against you.
